reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Lists & Tuples
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 4. Up to now, many of our variables have held one value at a time. Lists and tuples let us organize several related values inside one object.

That matters in analytics because we usually work with collections: several scores, several sales values, several ages, or several records.

[tts-break]

We’ll learn how to create these collections, access individual values, update lists, loop through them, summarize them, and decide when a list or tuple is the better choice.

slides.title: How to use this page
slides.transcript:
Work through the examples by reading the idea, running the code, and then making a small change.

With collections, small edits are especially useful. Add one value, remove one value, change an index, or adjust a slice and watch what happens.

[tts-break]

Try to describe the result before you run the cell. That habit helps you understand how Python is organizing the data instead of relying on trial and error.

slides.title: Learning path for Module 4
slides.transcript:
We begin with lists, which store multiple values in order. Then we use indexes and slices to retrieve specific parts of a list.

Next, we modify lists, loop through them, and summarize numeric values. After that, tuples give us a similar ordered structure that is intended to stay fixed.

[tts-break]

By the end, you should be able to look at a data task and decide whether you need a flexible list or a fixed tuple.

slides.title: Why sequences matter in analytics
slides.transcript:
One observation is rarely enough in analytics. We usually want to work with a sequence of related values.

A list is ordered and mutable, meaning we can change it. A tuple is ordered too, but it is intended to remain fixed. An index gives us a position number for accessing one value.

[tts-break]

Think about five exam scores or a week of daily sales. A sequence lets us store those values together and then summarize, filter, or process them as one collection.

slides.title: Create a list
slides.transcript:
Let’s create a list of five scores.

The square brackets tell Python that these values belong to one list. Printing the list shows the full collection. Len tells us there are five values. Max returns ninety-one, and min returns sixty-nine.

[tts-break]

A list is a good choice here because scores may be added, removed, sorted, or updated later.

Try adding another score and rerun the summary functions. Notice that the same code adapts to the larger collection.

slides.title: Index and slice a list
slides.transcript:
Python uses zero-based indexing, so the first value is at position zero.

Scores zero returns eighty-two. Scores one returns seventy-six. A negative one means the last value, which is sixty-nine.

A slice lets us retrieve several values. Scores one through four starts at index one and stops before index four, giving seventy-six, ninety-one, and eighty-eight.

[tts-break]

The stop position is excluded. That detail appears throughout Python, so it is worth getting comfortable with early.

slides.title: Change a list
slides.transcript:
Lists are mutable, which means we can change them after they are created.

We start with twenty-one, nineteen, and twenty-four visits. Append adds twenty-seven to the end. Then index one is changed from nineteen to twenty.

Pop zero removes the first value, twenty-one, and also returns it so we can store it in removed_value.

[tts-break]

Run the example one line at a time mentally. The final list should contain twenty, twenty-four, and twenty-seven.

This ability to grow and change is one of the main reasons to use a list.

slides.title: Loop through a list
slides.transcript:
Now we combine lists with the control flow from Module 2.

The loop takes one wait time at a time. If the value is greater than ten minutes, the program labels it for review. Otherwise it labels the wait as acceptable.

[tts-break]

For the current values, eleven and eighteen should be flagged for review. Four, seven, and six should be acceptable.

This is the bridge from storing a collection to actually analyzing each observation in it.

slides.title: Summarize values in a list
slides.transcript:
Lists work naturally with built-in summary functions.

The four monthly sales values add to fifty-three thousand two hundred. Dividing by four gives an average of thirteen thousand three hundred. Max identifies fourteen thousand nine hundred as the best month.

[tts-break]

The pattern is simple but important: collect values, calculate a summary, then interpret it.

Later, Pandas will give us more advanced summary tools, but the underlying logic is the same.

slides.title: Create and unpack a tuple
slides.transcript:
A tuple is another ordered collection, but it is designed for values that should stay together and not be changed casually.

The example stores latitude and longitude as one location tuple. Python can then unpack those two values into separate variables.

[tts-break]

This works nicely for fixed records such as coordinates, a pair of summary statistics, or several results returned from a function.

The tuple still supports indexing, so position zero gives the latitude.

slides.title: Lists can hold tuples
slides.transcript:
Collections can be combined. Here we have a list of transaction records, and each record is a tuple containing an ID and an amount.

The loop unpacks each tuple into transaction_id and amount, then prints the record.

After that, a list comprehension extracts only the amounts so we can sum them.

[tts-break]

This structure is a simple table-like representation: several rows in a list, with fixed fields inside each row.

Later, Pandas will give us a more powerful table structure, but this is a useful bridge.

slides.title: Small practice steps
slides.transcript:
This practice example combines several list operations in one short workflow.

We begin with ages twenty-three, thirty-one, and twenty-nine. Append adds forty-two. Pop removes the last value, so forty-two comes back out and the list returns to the original three ages.

[tts-break]

The average of twenty-three, thirty-one, and twenty-nine is about twenty-seven point seven.

Try changing the numbers or removing a different position. The goal is to become comfortable predicting how the list changes after each operation.

slides.title: Patient-age list management
slides.transcript:
Here is a small example of a list growing as a new record arrives.

The starting ages are forty-four, fifty-seven, thirty-nine, and sixty-three. We append fifty-one, so the list now contains five values.

The loop then builds a second list containing only ages above fifty. That should include fifty-seven, sixty-three, and fifty-one.

[tts-break]

Notice that we are using one list as the source and another list as the filtered result. That pattern appears frequently in data preparation.

These are generic fictional records, not real patient data.

slides.title: List + tuple capstone
slides.transcript:
This example combines a list, a function, and a tuple return value.

Summarize_range receives a list of weekly sales. It finds the lowest value, the highest value, and the spread between them. Those three results are returned together as a tuple.

For the current data, the low is thirty-nine hundred, the high is sixty-one hundred, and the range is twenty-two hundred.

[tts-break]

The caller then unpacks those results into three variables. This is a clean way to package several related summary values.

slides.title: Choose the right sequence
slides.transcript:
The choice between a list and a tuple depends on how you expect the data to behave.

Use a list when values may be added, removed, sorted, or updated. Use a tuple when the values form a fixed record or when you want to return several results that belong together.

[tts-break]

A simple rule is: lists are flexible collections; tuples are fixed records.

That rule will cover many beginner use cases.

slides.title: Key takeaways
slides.transcript:
Let’s bring the sequence concepts together.

Lists are ordered and mutable. Indexes give access to individual positions. Slices retrieve ranges. Loops let us process each value. Tuples are ordered but intended to remain fixed.

[tts-break]

You can now organize multiple values and write small workflows that summarize or filter collections.

Next, dictionaries and sets will give us structures for labeled values and unique values.

[tts-break]

Module 5 moves from position-based collections to labeled and unique data. We’ll use dictionaries to represent records with meaningful keys, and sets to work with unique values, duplicates, and group comparisons. Those structures are especially useful as our examples start to look more like real datasets.
